catalog_quote: The penultimate syllable of a prosodic phrase is normally lengthened
sweep_summary: Two works with stress in the title for Tswana. (1) Mosaka 2000 (SAJAL 20(2): 177-185, doi 10.1080/02572117.2000.10587424) is exactly a word-stress paper for Tswana (and Xhosa) but is closed access everywhere checked (T&F/Sabinet 403, Unpaywall not OA, S2 CLOSED with abstract elided, no OpenAlex/archive.org/Google Books trace); two open UCT theses by Mahura (2014 MSc p. 36; 2021 PhD pp. 55-56, both saved) summarise it as treating penultimate lengthening as fixed penultimate stress, with additional initial-syllable lengthening, while contrasting Cole 1955's view that the penultimate prominence is length without stress function. Priority high to acquire (library/T&F). (2) Zerbian & Barnard 2010 (ISCA, downloaded and read) is a word-level TONE algorithm, silent on word-stress placement; its one relevant line says intonation-phrase boundaries determine where penultimate lengthening falls, which supports the catalog's correction note that Tswana sources describe phrase-level prominence. Nothing read supersedes the catalog's deciding source (Bennett et al. 2016 JIPA p. 244, already held by the project, quote verified verbatim); catalog's classification fixed-dominant (penultimate) stands.

new_statements.locator: p. 2 (PDF page 2), paragraph following example (5), section 'Prosodic boundaries'
new_statements.reading: Penultimate lengthening (the phenomenon the catalog codes as Tswana's fixed penultimate 'stress') is placed by intonation-phrase boundaries, not by word boundaries; the authors treat Sotho-Tswana word-level prosody as tone, with no word-stress statement at all. This is the only new first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title; it is weaker as a stress source than the catalog's existing Bennett et al. 2016 (JIPA 46(2): 244) / Cole 1955: 55 chain and does not replace them. The one title that promises a genuine word-stress analysis of Tswana, Mosaka 2000, could not be opened (paywalled; no OA copy anywhere).

sources.quote: "Full length occurs in the penultimate syllable of a word pronounced in isolation or at the end of a sentence.... This constitutes the characteristic penultimate accent of Tswana.... When a word is in non-final sentence position, it still retains its penultimate accent, but in much lesser degree, i.e. only half-length is used. Normal short length occurs in final and non-penultimate syllables, and in some monosyllabic words." (Cole 1955:55, quoted verbatim in Hyman 2009:197-198). Also Coetzee 200

sources.locator: p. 2, section on prosodic boundaries (after example (5)); p. 3, discussion
sources.note: The paper is an algorithm for word-level TONE assignment in Sotho-Tswana (H/L tone rules, sandhi, phrase-boundary Finality rule); it contains no statement of word-stress placement. Its only prominence remark is that penultimate lengthening (with a falling tone) is located by intonation-phrase boundaries, i.e. it is a phrase-level, not word-level, phenomenon; p. 3 adds that yes/no questions lack penultimate lengthening (impressionistically, as in Xhosa). This supports the catalog's correction note that Tswana's source statements describe phrase-level prominence, not word stress.
